children: Nvidia-backed cloud computing company Nscale filed for an initial public offering.
The U.K.-based company didn't say how many shares it would offer, or at what price, according to a Friday filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The startup, which operates a series of data centers in the U.S. and Europe, is backed by Nvidia, Dell Technologies, and Nokia, as well as Aker, a Norwegian industrial investment group. It raised $2 billion at a $14.6 billion valuation earlier this year.
It intends to apply to list shares on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol NSCL.

A former top OpenAI executive, Fidji Simo, recently joined the company's board at the invitation of Sheryl Sandberg, the former Meta Platforms executive and another Nscale board member, ahead of a potential IPO, The Wall Street Journal reported last week.

Nscale's initial public offering would aim to capitalize on a wave of investor interest in companies providing data centers and the land and power necessary for them to operatem. The company's founder and chief executive, Josh Payne, said that Nscale represents a fully vertically-integrated platform that can deliver computing power to the AI boom at scale.

"Own the land, the power, the data center, the chips and the software," Payne wrote in a letter included in the filing. "Delivered end-to-end in a single unified system, purpose-built from the ground up to deliver speed, performance, and efficiency on the most demanding AI workloads."

Nscale reported a loss of $1.02 billion on $140.6 million in revenue for the first six months of this year, according to the filing. That compares with a $368.9 million loss on $10.4 million in revenue in the same period a year earlier.
In July, the company said it secured a $900 million revolving credit facility from a consortium of banks to help support its data center buildout.
It also recently signed a $45 billion deal to rent Nvidia hardware to Anthropic and agreed to buy the AI software company Anyscale, according to the Journal.

The company had 55 information technology megawatts worth of active computing capacity as of last month, with more than 10 gigawatts of potential data center capacity, according to the filing. It had around $103 billion in active and contracted total contract value as of August.
